messages.subject: Independence of chains, can different RNGs be used?
messages.subject_clean: Independence of chains, can different RNGs be used?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I'm coming from JAGS, which was ensuring that the chains are independent by using four different
Random Number Generators for each chain (see chapter 3.3.2 in JAGS manual):

"base::Wichmann-Hill"
"base::Marsaglia-Multicarry"
"base::Super-Duper"
"base::Mersenne-Twister" (my R uses this as default, see also RNGking() and ?Random)

JAGS will automatically assign a different RNG to each chain, and in parallel processing, where
JAGS is processing just one chain in each instance, the name of the RNG could be specified in initial values by setting `.RNG.name` variable.

In Nimble, is there such a possibility? How does Nimble ensure the independence of chains, in
normal and in parallel run, where Nimble is run in 3 separate instances? (as here: https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/parallelizing_NIMBLE.html).

Thanks and best regards!

Tomas

messages.subject: Re: Vectorize Zero-truncated Poisson Density Computation
messages.subject_clean: Vectorize Zero-truncated Poisson Density Computation
messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

It looks like your dtpois takes in a scalar but in dTruncPoissonVector you are passing in a vector to dtpois.

You can change dTruncPoissonVector to have a for loop that calls dtpois, if you want to keep the modularity you have, but my suggestion would be to have a single vectorized distribution that takes in vector x and does the truncated Poisson calculation in a vectorized fashion internally without calling out to a scalar distribution function. (That said, since this will be compiled, using a for loop within dTruncPoissVector that directly does the calculations you have in dtpois should be just as fast.)

-chris

On Wed, Dec 1, 2021 at 10:41 PM Ben Lee <benl...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hello,
>
> In the past, I was able to speed up computation by vectorizing operations such as the density calculation for iid Bernoulli random variables:
>
> dBernoulliVector <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(x    = double(1),
>                  prob = double(1),
>                  log  = integer(0, default = 0)) { ## default should be zero
>     returnType(double(0))
>     logProb <- sum(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = prob, log = TRUE))
>     if(log) return(logProb) else return(exp(logProb))
>   }
> )
>
> Is there a way for me to vectorize operations for Zero-truncated Poisson random variables?  I tried doing the following, but it doesn't seem to work:
>
> dtpois <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(x = integer(), lambda = double(),
>                  log = logical(0, default = 0)) {
>     returnType(double())
>     ## First handle non-zero data
>     if(x==0){
>       if(log){
>         return(-Inf)
>       }else{
>         return(0)
>       }
>
>     }else{
>       if (log){
>         return(dpois(x, lambda, log = TRUE) - log(1-exp(-lambda)))
>       }else{
>         return(dpois(x, lambda, log = FALSE)/(1-exp(-lambda)))
>       }
>     }
>
>   })
>
> rtpois <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(n = integer(), lambda = double()) {
>     returnType(integer())
>     return(rpois(1, lambda)+1) # This was a lazy fix. I just added this component for completeness. I do not intend to sample from this distribution.
>   })
>
> registerDistributions(list(
>   dtpois = list(
>     BUGSdist = "dtpois(lambda)",
>     discrete = TRUE,
>     range = c(0, Inf),
>     types = c('value = integer()', 'lambda = double()')
>   )))
>
>
> dTruncPoissonVector <- nimbleFunction(
>   run = function(x    = double(1),
>                  lambda = double(1),
>                  log  = integer(0, default = 0)) { ## default should be zero
>
>
>     returnType(double(0))
>     logProb <- sum(dtpois(x, lambda = lambda, log = TRUE))
>     if(log) return(logProb) else return(exp(logProb))
>   }
> )
>
>
> Thank you so much!
>
>

messages.subject: age-structured CJS model in nimble
messages.subject_clean: age-structured CJS model in nimble
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am pretty new to Nimble with some experience with JAGS (and jagsUI package).
I want to calculate WAIC to do model selection on different age-structured CJS models. That is why I decided to convert my JAGS codes to Nimble.
The code is adapted from Kery and Schaub's Bayesian Population Analysis Using WinBUGS book, section 7.7.

For my global (most complex model) I am trying to calculate survival and recapture rates for 2-age levels (Juvenile and Adult), 2-sexes (Female and Male), and 2-seasons (Dry and Wet). Recapture probability function also has random year effect.
I calculate the desired derived parameters inside the model. (see attached code global_x.R and some data to run it data_x.R)

It looks like model runs smoothly, however since I want to get WAIC, I am also monitoring the p and z values of the likelihood in my parameters of interest, and when I try to check diagnostics of z (sometimes p too with other models not the global one) with MCMCsummary or MCMCtrace functions like so

MCMCsummary(out_p1global$samples, params = "z", round=3)
MCMCtrace(out_p1global$samples, params = "z", pdf=F, ind = T, Rhat = T, n.eff = T)

it gives me an error as:
"Error in quantile.default(newX[, i], ...) :
  missing values and NaN's not allowed if 'na.rm' is FALSE"

I tried to look what is wrong by checking the values of z in the first chain as:
temp.z <- out_p1global$samples[[1]][,grep("z", colnames(out_p1global$samples[[1]]))]
and it looks like the first row has NAs. I have NAs in the age matrix covariate (agemat) until the first capture (logically), I have NAs in the initial values of until the next time step of the first capture (again logically). Finally, I have NAs in the initial values of slopes wherever I fixed them to a value in the model.

I try all my models first with these MCMC settings
ni <- 10; nt <- 1 ; nb <- 5 ; nc <- 3 .

So, to solve the issue I tried:
1. same model without asking for WAIC, got the same error.
2. Run the same model with WAIC with better MCMC settings and longer iterations
na <- 5000 ; ni <- 150000; nt <- 20 ; nb <-5000 ; nc <- 3, got the same error.

I also ran the same model with same MCMC settings in JAGS as well and the estimates from JAGS and Nimble were same, so I'm guessing this might not be a coding error in the model?

My questions are
Any idea how to solve this issue?
Only reason I am monitoring p and z is WAIC. Can I trust the calculated WAIC?
Again, since I don't need the estimates of p and z anyway, does this issue matter for the rest of my parameter estimates if their diagnostics are fine? Can I still use estimates to calculate predictions even if I get this error for z and p (sometimes both of them depending on the model)?
Thank you for all the help in advance, sorry for rather long message.
Best,
Dilsad

Dear ALL;

I exactly follow the link about Rtools from here: https://r-nimble.org/download. pumpCode <- nimbleCode({
  for (i in 1:N){
    theta[i] ~ dgamma(alpha,beta)
    lambda[i] <- theta[i]*t[i]
    x[i] ~ dpois(lambda[i])

messages.subject: Re: Independence of chains, can different RNGs be used?
messages.subject_clean: Independence of chains, can different RNGs be used?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Tomas,

When you follow the code in that example <https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/parallelizing_NIMBLE.html> of running chains in parallel, one is simply setting a different seed for each chain. This is similar to JAGS once JAGS gets to a fifth chain (after using different generators for the first four).
By default, runMCMC and nimbleMCMC just have the random number generation for each chain pick up where the previous chain left off, which of course guarantees independence. But if you use setSeed, then that will also set different seeds for each chain.

In general, setting different seeds is very likely to be fine. It's hard to find reliable information about this, but my understanding is that different seeds should be quite far apart in the period sequence that random numbers generate. That said, it's possible that the pseudo-random numbers for two chains could overlap, but if this happened, it would happen such that the initial random numbers for one chain occurred at some point later in the sequence of numbers for the second chain. I doubt that this would cause any impactful dependence given that an MCMC will depend in a complex way on the full history of the chain.

But if you wanted to be safe, I have a (not nimble-related) tutorial <https://berkeley-scf.github.io/tutorial-parallelization/parallel-R#5-parallel-random-number-generation> on how to use the various tools in R to generate random numbers in parallel. You could combine those tools with the NIMBLE parallelization example linked to above.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Perry,
Thanks for getting back to me. You are correct, the chains were short just as an example of the  model. As you noted the mark-recapture part of the model is converging. Per your suggestions, I modified the code to run the chains in parallel, initialized more parameters, ran the model for more iterations (niter=210000, nburnin=10000, thin=100) with convergence issues (Rhat > 1.2 and n.eff<100) for some parameters in the proper CAR model.  There is poor mixing of the chains in gamma[2], sig[1], sig[2], and cor12. I pasted the CAR part of the code below.  As a reminder the parameter phi =  log of fish density. See attached trace and density plots..

One issue may be that I have not correctly implemented the CAR model for both years, as it was adapted from another source and may also need more informative priors. Thought? Thanks again for your help.
Dan

##############################################################
  #Proper CAR Model
  for (h in 1:yrs){
    S[h,1:s] ~ dcar_proper(mumod[1:s],C[1:L],adj[1:L],num[1:s],M[1:s],tauS[h],gamma[h]) #car proper use with build
    tauS[h]<-1
    gamma[h]~dunif(bou[1],bou[2])
  }

  #Wishart priors & equation for phi
  Prec[1:yrs,1:yrs]~dwish(R[1:yrs,1:yrs],yrs)
  Cov[1:yrs,1:yrs]<-inverse(Prec[1:yrs,1:yrs])
  Achol[1:yrs,1:yrs]<-t(chol(Cov[1:yrs,1:yrs]))
  for(i in 1:s){
    phi[1:yrs,i]<-Achol[1:yrs,1:yrs]%*%S[1:yrs,i]
    }

#Derived parameters
  sig[1]<-sqrt(Cov[1,1])
  sig[2]<-sqrt(Cov[2,2])
  cor12<-Cov[1,2]/(sig[1]*sig[2])
###############################################

On Mon, Nov 15, 2021 at 3:36 PM Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> Hi Dan,
>
> I looked through your code and ran it.  I don't know this model well, but I think I roughly followed it.
>
> I don't see something that is not working in terms of MCMC machinery or obvious changes in strategy.  Your chains looked very short to me.  I ran them for much longer (10x, and you might consider 100x), with some thinning (and possibly use monitors2 as well), and lots of nodes seemed to be mixing.
>
> I did not see mixing for most of the theta elements, but that seemed to make sense.  It looks like those are sets of Dirichlet-distributed vectors with priors making it extremely likely that there is no movement between strata, so there will be one 1 and the rest 0, or nearly so, in each vector.  That makes sense because the data seem to show only a handful of movements between strata.  I am not clear if there is much information in the data on movement and hence much useful estimation that can happen here or if you are comfortable more or less imposing the movement probabilities or if I'm not following this part.  But from an MCMC perspective, it seems to make sense that when there are mostly 0s for how many fish moved strata, and when the prior says strongly that there is nearly no chance of moving, then the posterior will say there is nearly no chance of moving, and all of those theta elements be essentially 0 all the time.  If I look at a cell of theta corresponding (I think) to some of the few movements in the data (e.g. "theta[2, 4, 7]"), it mixes with non-zero probabilities.
>
> It can be important to initialize all unobserved nodes, but sometimes it works fine not to.
>
> HTH
>
> -Perry
>

> On Wed, Nov 10, 2021 at 10:16 AM drfi...@gmail.com <drfi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > All,
> > I was hoping to get some assistance on improving the speed and convergence of a multiyear mark-recapture CAR model.
> >
> > Model
> > A study was conducted on a stream with 17 contiguous strata, where juvenile salmonids were captured, marked, and released. The stream was resampled at a later time where fish marked and unmarked fish were enumerated. If there was no movement between strata, this could be analyzed using a simple Lincoln/Petersen closed population model. However, there was movement between strata and a better approach is to analyzed the data using a Darroch model, which is a multistate model that allows movement or transition between the strata.
> >
> > Rather than estimate strata adundance (n*) directly, we assume the abundance is a Poisson distributed based on the product of the density (fish/meter) and the area in meters of each strata. I could analyze this as a hierarchical model where log(lambda[i])~Normal(mu_phi,tau_phi). However, this would not account for spatial dependence between adjacent stream reaches, which can be analyzed using a proper CAR model.
> >
> > To add a level of complexity, I have two years of data that I would like to analyze simultaneously and eventually model density as a function of covariates. The current model has very high autocorrelation, low effective sample size. and poor convergence. Given the model complexity, I could not initialize all nodes and settled for one that would not crash the model. I would appreciate any advice on different samplers or code modification that would improve convergence and speed but am at a loss on where to start given the different distributions and my inexperience with NIMBLE.  Code and data are attached. Thanks!
> >
> > Dan

Dear Dan

I have only looked at your trace plots and have not looked at the details of your model. But it is quite clear that there are very strong correlations between certain pairs of parameters. Have you tried the cross-correlation plot in the coda package? I suspect if you do then you'll see correlations very close to one - because some parameters have near identical trace plots.  These very strong relations  suggest non-identifiability in your model. This would point to a need to re-parameterise things a little bit.

Hope that helps
David

messages.subject_clean: How to 'extend' existing MCMC calculation in nimble?
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

say that I do MCMC calculation and figure out I need more iterations, is there a way to extend existing MCMC calculation, as it was possible in JAGS? Thanks. I tried to look into ?runMCMC, but I only found this note:

The MCMC option mcmc$run(..., reset = FALSE), used to continue execution of an MCMC chain, is not available through runMCMC().

But there isn't a reference to how it is possible now. Or does it mean it was possible before and isn't any more?

Thanks,

Tomas

messages.subject: Re: How to 'extend' existing MCMC calculation in nimble?
messages.subject_clean: How to 'extend' existing MCMC calculation in nimble?
messages.body_plain:
Tomas, if you've already used runMCMC(Cmcmc, ...), then yes, you can still extend the current MCMC chain, using:

Cmcmc$run(niter, reset = FALSE)

where niter is the number of additional MCMC iterations you wish to run.  After that, you can extract the full maxtrix of MCMC samples (which will include the ones you previously executed in the first call of runMCMC), using:

full_matrix_of_samples <- as.matrix(Cmcmc$mvSamples)

I hope this answers your question.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
I think I am having the same/similar issue as the original post here. I'm aiming to have a WAIC value calculated from all chains run in parallel. Nimble has since updated with the online method of WAIC calculation, so I have been able to compute a WAIC efficiently within my parallel model function, which then gets repeated in parallel using parLapply() and I end up with essentially a perChainWAIC. Is there a valid way to 'average' these into a single value? (or can these not be used beyond "as a means of helping assess the stability of the WAIC estimate"? as in runMCMC help) Alternatively, the workaround method suggested in this thread is not working for me, for some reason that I don't understand? I don't include here my parallel function code and parLapply, but the chain_output objects come directly from that, with longer chains. This code is setting and running the model for a non-zero number of iterations in the global environment.

Thank you in advance if you can offer any advice or solutions,

Michael

y <- matrix(sample(c(0,1),120,replace = TRUE),ncol = 6, nrow = 20)
first <- apply(y, 1, function(x) min(which(x!= 0),na.rm = TRUE))

hmm.model<- nimbleCode({

  # Priors
  phi ~ dunif(0,1)    # prior for survival φ
  p ~ dunif(0,1)      # prior for detection p

  # Vector of initial state probabilities δ
  delta[1] <- 1     # Alive
  delta[2] <- 0     # Dead

  # Transition matrix Γ
  gamma[1,1] <- phi     # transition Pr(alive T t --> alive T t+1)
  gamma[1,2] <- 1-phi    # transition Pr(alive T t --> alive R t+1)
  gamma[2,1] <- 0     # transition Pr(alive R t --> alive T t+1)
  gamma[2,2] <- 1   # transition Pr(alive R t --> alive R t+1)

  # Observation matrix Ω
  omega[1,1] <- 1 - p # observation Pr(alive T t --> not detected t)
  omega[1,2] <- p     # observation Pr(alive T t --> detected t)
  omega[2,1] <- 1 # observation Pr(alive R t --> not detected t)
  omega[2,2] <- 0     # observation Pr(alive R t --> detected t)

  # Likelihood
  for(i in 1:N){    # Loops over each individual (row)
    z[i,first[i]] ~ dcat(delta[1:2])  # Draws an initial state
    for(j in (first[i]+1):T){    # Loops through each time point (column)
      z[i,j] ~ dcat(gamma[z[i,j-1], 1:2]) # Draws current state based on previous state
      y[i,j] ~ dcat(omega[z[i,j], 1:2])  # Draws an observation based on current state.
    }
  }
})

# Defines constants in the model
my.constants <- list(N = nrow(y),   # N individual
                     T = ncol(y),   # N of time points
                     first = first) # occasions of first capture

# Defines data in the model
# To remove 0s. 1 is non-detected, 2 is detected
my.data <- list(y = y+1)

# Defines initial values for states and probabilities
zinits <- y + 1
zinits[zinits == 2] <- 1

initial.values <-  list(phi = runif(1,0,1),
                        p = runif(1,0,1),
                        z = zinits)

# Specfies the parameters of interest to record in output
parameters.to.save <- c("phi","p")

#MCMC model details
n.iter <- 10 # non-zero number of iterations
n.burnin <- 2

myModel <- nimbleModel(code = hmm.model,
                       constants = my.constants,
                       data = my.data,
                       inits = initial.values)

CmyModel <- compileNimble(myModel)

myMCMC <- buildMCMC(CmyModel, monitors = parameters.to.save, enableWAIC = TRUE)

CmyMCMC <- compileNimble(myMCMC)

results <- runMCMC(CmyMCMC, niter = n.iter, nburnin = n.burnin, nchains = 1)

posteriorSamplesMatrix <- rbind(chain_output[[1]],

                                chain_output[[2]],
                                chain_output[[3]],
                                chain_output[[4]],
                                chain_output[[5]])

CmyMCMC$run(5)   ## non-zero number of iterations
nimble:::matrix2mv(posteriorSamplesMatrix, CmyMCMC$mvSamples)
CmyMCMC$enableWAIC <- TRUE
CmyMCMC$calculateWAIC()

## The following gets returned:
> CmyMCMC$mvSamples CmodelValues object with variables: p, phi.
> CmyMCMC$run(5)
NULL
> CmyMCMC$calculateWAIC()
NA
# Existing chain ouput
> head(chain_output[[1]]) p phi [1,] 0.5465156 0.9609154 [2,] 0.5465156 0.9609154 [3,] 0.5465156 0.9609154 [4,] 0.5465156 0.9609154 [5,] 0.5465156 0.9609154 [6,] 0.5465156 0.9609154 > str(chain_output[[1]]) num [1:800, 1:2] 0.547 0.547 0.547 0.547 0.547 ... - attr(*, "dimnames")=List of 2 ..$ : NULL ..$ : chr [1:2] "p" "phi"

messages.body_plain:
hi Dilsad,

Sorry about the late reply - this one "fell through the cracks".

A few thoughts here:

1) WAIC uses the likelihood at each iteration (since v. 0.12.0, if using the new "online" WAIC we offer) or the likelihood at each monitored sample (in earlier versions). Since the likelihood for 'y' depends on 'p' and 'z', the key thing is that the likelihood not be NA. When I run your code, I see that the likelihood can be calculated once the initial values are set even though there are some NA values for some elements of 'z'. So I think the WAIC calculation should be fine.

2) If you have some elements of z that are deterministic and not used, then I don't think it makes sense to try and summarize their posterior samples as you are doing. I would only check the MCMC mixing of the z's that are stochastic and being sampled.

The p's are deterministic. For those that are not fixed to be constant values, but instead depend on other parameters that are being sampled, it's fine to check their mixing if you want to.

3) Since the z and p values that are given NA are not ever used, you could probably just set them to 0 without any ill effects and then you wouldn't see the warnings about NAs when you use the MCMCvis  package functions on the monitored values of all the z's and all the p's, which includes those that are not being sampled and for which the diagnostics are not meaningful.

I might not have fully followed what the issue is, so feel free to follow up.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Michael,

If you use runMCMC or nimbleMCMC with multiple chains, we'll compute a single WAIC from all the chains by default.

Unfortunately, if you are running in parallel, you'll have to do a bit of extra work to get a single WAIC using the samples from your separately-run parallel chains. You should use the current nimble (version 0.12.1). This will use an "offline" version of WAIC that does all the WAIC calculations after the fact, rather than the default WAIC that does calculations at each iteration.

1) Set up your MCMC so that you monitor all of the variables that are involved in the likelihood. Do not set the WAIC argument to runMCMC or nimbleMCMC, just let it default to FALSE.

2) Once you've run the MCMC chains, collect the samples from them as separate matrices. Discard any burn-in, if you haven't already, and then rbind the matrices together so you have as many rows as the total number of samples across all the chains. Then use the `calculateWAIC` function, passing the matrix of samples as the first argument and the model object as the second argument.

-chris

> hi Dilsad,
>
> Sorry about the late reply - this one "fell through the cracks".
>
> A few thoughts here:
>
> 1) WAIC uses the likelihood at each iteration (since v. 0.12.0, if using the new "online" WAIC we offer) or the likelihood at each monitored sample (in earlier versions). Since the likelihood for 'y' depends on 'p' and 'z', the key thing is that the likelihood not be NA. When I run your code, I see that the likelihood can be calculated once the initial values are set even though there are some NA values for some elements of 'z'. So I think the WAIC calculation should be fine.
>
> 2) If you have some elements of z that are deterministic and not used, then I don't think it makes sense to try and summarize their posterior samples as you are doing. I would only check the MCMC mixing of the z's that are stochastic and being sampled.
>
> The p's are deterministic. For those that are not fixed to be constant values, but instead depend on other parameters that are being sampled, it's fine to check their mixing if you want to.
>
> 3) Since the z and p values that are given NA are not ever used, you could probably just set them to 0 without any ill effects and then you wouldn't see the warnings about NAs when you use the MCMCvis  package functions on the monitored values of all the z's and all the p's, which includes those that are not being sampled and for which the diagnostics are not meaningful.
>
> I might not have fully followed what the issue is, so feel free to follow up.
>
> -chris

This will use an "offline" version of WAIC that does all the WAIC calculations after the fact, rather than the default WAIC that does calculations at each iteration.
>
> 1) Set up your MCMC so that you monitor all of the variables that are involved in the likelihood. Do not set the WAIC argument to runMCMC or nimbleMCMC, just let it default to FALSE.
>
> 2) Once you've run the MCMC chains, collect the samples from them as separate matrices. Discard any burn-in, if you haven't already, and then rbind the matrices together so you have as many rows as the total number of samples across all the chains. messages.body_plain:
Hi Tomas,

This <https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11222-013-9416-2/> is a good reference to see how WAIC is calculated and what the impact of averaging the per chain values would be. It won't get the same values as treating it as a single chain.

-chris

On Mon, Dec 13, 2021 at 6:37 AM Tomas T. <tomas.t...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Dear Chris, thanks for this info, so is it not correct to just simply average the WAIC, lppd and pWAIC values from parallel chains? As we do with other estimates? That's what I've been doing up till now. When the model converges, the values from the chains are usually very similar. Perhaps this average should then converge to the correctly calculated WAIC?
>
> I am asking because the approach you described (to monitor all nodes) might result in quite huge sample matrices, much bigger than the values we actually want to monitor. This sound quite inconvenient, so I am trying to find out if the lazy solution wouldn't just work nicely for well-converged models.
>
> Thanks,
>
> Tomas
>
> On Sat, 11 Dec 2021 at 00:58, Chris Paciorek <christophe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Michael,
> >
> > If you use runMCMC or nimbleMCMC with multiple chains, we'll compute a single WAIC from all the chains by default.
> >
> > Unfortunately, if you are running in parallel, you'll have to do a bit of extra work to get a single WAIC using the samples from your separately-run parallel chains. You should use the current nimble (version 0.12.1). This will use an "offline" version of WAIC that does all the WAIC calculations after the fact, rather than the default WAIC that does calculations at each iteration.
> >
> > 1) Set up your MCMC so that you monitor all of the variables that are involved in the likelihood. Do not set the WAIC argument to runMCMC or nimbleMCMC, just let it default to FALSE.
> >
> > 2) Once you've run the MCMC chains, collect the samples from them as separate matrices. Discard any burn-in, if you haven't already, and then rbind the matrices together so you have as many rows as the total number of samples across all the chains. Then use the `calculateWAIC` function, passing the matrix of samples as the first argument and the model object as the second argument.
> >
> > -chris
> >
> >
> > On Fri, Dec 10, 2021 at 5:05 AM Michael Roast <michae...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > I think I am having the same/similar issue as the original post here. I'm aiming to have a WAIC value calculated from all chains run in parallel. Nimble has since updated with the online method of WAIC calculation, so I have been able to compute a WAIC efficiently within my parallel model function, which then gets repeated in parallel using parLapply() and I end up with essentially a perChainWAIC. Is there a valid way to 'average' these into a single value? (or can these not be used beyond "as a means of helping assess the stability of the WAIC estimate"? as in runMCMC help) Alternatively, the workaround method suggested in this thread is not working for me, for some reason that I don't understand? I don't include here my parallel function code and parLapply, but the chain_output objects come directly from that, with longer chains. This code is setting and running the model for a non-zero number of iterations in the global environment.
> > >
> > > Thank you in advance if you can offer any advice or solutions,
> > >
> > > Michael
> > >
> > >
> > > y <- matrix(sample(c(0,1),120,replace = TRUE),ncol = 6, nrow = 20)
> > > first <- apply(y, 1, function(x) min(which(x!= 0),na.rm = TRUE))
> > >
> > > hmm.model<- nimbleCode({
> > >
> > >   # Priors
> > >   phi ~ dunif(0,1)    # prior for survival φ
> > >   p ~ dunif(0,1)      # prior for detection p
> > >
> > >   # Vector of initial state probabilities δ
> > >   delta[1] <- 1     # Alive
> > >   delta[2] <- 0     # Dead
> > >
> > >   # Transition matrix Γ
> > >   gamma[1,1] <- phi     # transition Pr(alive T t --> alive T t+1)
> > >   gamma[1,2] <- 1-phi    # transition Pr(alive T t --> alive R t+1)
> > >   gamma[2,1] <- 0     # transition Pr(alive R t --> alive T t+1)
> > >   gamma[2,2] <- 1   # transition Pr(alive R t --> alive R t+1)
> > >
> > >   # Observation matrix Ω
> > >   omega[1,1] <- 1 - p # observation Pr(alive T t --> not detected t)
> > >   omega[1,2] <- p     # observation Pr(alive T t --> detected t)
> > >   omega[2,1] <- 1 # observation Pr(alive R t --> not detected t)
> > >   omega[2,2] <- 0     # observation Pr(alive R t --> detected t)
> > >
> > >   # Likelihood
> > >   for(i in 1:N){    # Loops over each individual (row)

> > >     for(j in (first[i]+1):T){    # Loops through each time point (column)

> > >     }
> > >   }
> > > })

> > > > > You're correct, you're run into a shortcoming of NIMBLE's current system for WAIC.  We're aware of this, and there's recently been much development effort put towards a new approach to WAIC calculations in NIMBLE.
> > > > >
> > > > > That said, you've done a nice job working around the current short-comings.  Just a few comments:

> > > > >
> > > > > - Using your approach, you'll either need to set enableWAIC = TRUE when you create the global version of the MCMC:

messages.body_plain:
hi Paritosh,

Recursion should work in nimbleFunctions. In fact, it does work in nimbleFunctions with setup code. However your code does not have setup code. Our compilation system handles nimbleFunctions with and without setup code somewhat differently, so we'll have to look into why this particular case fails.

The following modification of your nimbleFunction should work if you are just writing a stand-alone nimbleFunction. However, if you need to use this nimbleFunction in a model, you'll probably run into problems. I'll file a bug report for us to look into fixing the problem affecting your original formulation.

nimble_recursive_factorial_gen <- nimbleFunction(
  setup = TRUE,
  run = function(x=double(0)){
       returnType(double(0))
       if(x==0 | x==1) {
        return(1)
       }  else {
           return(x*run(x-1))
       }
})

                                             showCompilerOutput = TRUE)
nimble_recursive_factorial$run(4)

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thanks again for your solution and taking the time to help, it all makes sense to me. This works fine for the toy model I made, but I don't think it will be feasible with the hidden markov models (HMM) that I'm using on my much larger real dataset. Parallel computation of chains improves the processing speed, and calculating WAIC using the online method reduces the memory requirement, but if all the latent state nodes of a HMM must still be monitored during parallel computing of chains, then the memory is still a limiting factor that makes post-hoc WAIC calculation across all chains this way unfeasible. I guess there is still a computational limitation at the moment, where you can optimise processing or memory, but not at the same time to calculate the WAIC across chains for these models.

Many thanks,

Michael

messages.subject_clean: age-structured CJS model in nimble
messages.body_plain:
That's correct, I don't see any problems with using NIMBLE's WAIC here. Also note with the current version of nimble, you don't need to monitor any particular nodes. We now have an 'online' WAIC calculation that doesn't require monitors, so in fact you don't need to monitor p and z if you are not interested in them.

As far as convergence, that's a big question, and I didn't look in detail at your model from that perspective. Perhaps others on the list might have suggestions for these types of models. Trying different types of samplers, blocking parameters, reparameterizing, etc. could all be possibilities.
But you might first want to look at our nimbleEcology package, which provides a Cormack-Jolly-Seber model structure that might be helpful because it analytically integrates over the latent states so that the MCMC doesn't have to sample them. This has the potential to speed up the MCMC on a per-iteration basis and improve mixing by reducing the dimension of the parameter space and potentially reducing posterior correlation.

-chris

On Sun, Dec 12, 2021 at 3:19 AM Dilsad Dagtekin <dils...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Chris,
>
> Thanks for the really elaborated reply, it helped me to understand what the issue is a lot.
>
> I really do not think it is that important that I check the diagnostics of p and z anyway, because I do not use them for predictions etc. I monitor them only so that nimble can calculate WAIC. I am checking the traceplots of all the alphas and betas in the model to check the model diagnostics and then use the derived parameters for the main predictions from the model. I think based on what you are saying there is nothing wrong with doing this? And if all convergence issues are fine I can also trust WAIC for model selection right?
>
> Also, another issue is, models are actually not converging even with iterations more that 300k. I check traceplots of all alphas and betas, because I think these are the ones that needs to be good, and they look really bad. I also check Rhat, depending on the model it might be fine sometimes but still I trust traceplots more. I tried to change priors and come up with a solution, however so far I did not have any luck. When you ran the model, did you see anything weird or illogical that might cause that?
>
> Thanks.
> Best,
> Dilsad
>
> On Sat, Dec 11, 2021 at 12:47 AM Chris Paciorek <christophe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > hi Dilsad,
> >
> > Sorry about the late reply - this one "fell through the cracks".
> >
> > A few thoughts here:
> >
> > 1) WAIC uses the likelihood at each iteration (since v. 0.12.0, if using the new "online" WAIC we offer) or the likelihood at each monitored sample (in earlier versions). Since the likelihood for 'y' depends on 'p' and 'z', the key thing is that the likelihood not be NA. When I run your code, I see that the likelihood can be calculated once the initial values are set even though there are some NA values for some elements of 'z'. So I think the WAIC calculation should be fine.
> >
> > 2) If you have some elements of z that are deterministic and not used, then I don't think it makes sense to try and summarize their posterior samples as you are doing. I would only check the MCMC mixing of the z's that are stochastic and being sampled.
> >
> > The p's are deterministic. For those that are not fixed to be constant values, but instead depend on other parameters that are being sampled, it's fine to check their mixing if you want to.
> >
> > 3) Since the z and p values that are given NA are not ever used, you could probably just set them to 0 without any ill effects and then you wouldn't see the warnings about NAs when you use the MCMCvis  package functions on the monitored values of all the z's and all the p's, which includes those that are not being sampled and for which the diagnostics are not meaningful.
> >
> > I might not have fully followed what the issue is, so feel free to follow up.
> >
> > -chris
> >
> > On Fri, Dec 3, 2021 at 5:34 AM Dilsad Dagtekin <dils...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hi everyone,
> > >
> > > I am pretty new to Nimble with some experience with JAGS (and jagsUI package).
> > > I want to calculate WAIC to do model selection on different age-structured CJS models. That is why I decided to convert my JAGS codes to Nimble.
> > > The code is adapted from Kery and Schaub's Bayesian Population Analysis Using WinBUGS book, section 7.7.
> > >
> > > For my global (most complex model) I am trying to calculate survival and recapture rates for 2-age levels (Juvenile and Adult), 2-sexes (Female and Male), and 2-seasons (Dry and Wet). Recapture probability function also has random year effect.
> > > I calculate the desired derived parameters inside the model. (see attached code global_x.R and some data to run it data_x.R)
> > >
> > > It looks like model runs smoothly, however since I want to get WAIC, I am also monitoring the p and z values of the likelihood in my parameters of interest, and when I try to check diagnostics of z (sometimes p too with other models not the global one) with MCMCsummary or MCMCtrace functions like so
> > >
> > > MCMCsummary(out_p1global$samples, params = "z", round=3)
> > > MCMCtrace(out_p1global$samples, params = "z", pdf=F, ind = T, Rhat = T, n.eff = T)
> > >
> > > it gives me an error as:
> > > "Error in quantile.default(newX[, i], ...) :
> > >   missing values and NaN's not allowed if 'na.rm' is FALSE"
> > >
> > > I tried to look what is wrong by checking the values of z in the first chain as:
> > > temp.z <- out_p1global$samples[[1]][,grep("z", colnames(out_p1global$samples[[1]]))]
> > > and it looks like the first row has NAs. I have NAs in the age matrix covariate (agemat) until the first capture (logically), I have NAs in the initial values of until the next time step of the first capture (again logically). Finally, I have NAs in the initial values of slopes wherever I fixed them to a value in the model.
> > >
> > > I try all my models first with these MCMC settings
> > > ni <- 10; nt <- 1 ; nb <- 5 ; nc <- 3 .
> > >
> > > So, to solve the issue I tried:
> > > 1. same model without asking for WAIC, got the same error.
> > > 2. Run the same model with WAIC with better MCMC settings and longer iterations
> > > na <- 5000 ; ni <- 150000; nt <- 20 ; nb <-5000 ; nc <- 3, got the same error.
> > >
> > > I also ran the same model with same MCMC settings in JAGS as well and the estimates from JAGS and Nimble were same, so I'm guessing this might not be a coding error in the model?
> > >
> > > My questions are
> > > Any idea how to solve this issue?
> > > Only reason I am monitoring p and z is WAIC. Can I trust the calculated WAIC?
> > > Again, since I don't need the estimates of p and z anyway, does this issue matter for the rest of my parameter estimates if their diagnostics are fine? Can I still use estimates to calculate predictions even if I get this error for z and p (sometimes both of them depending on the model)?
> > > Thank you for all the help in advance, sorry for rather long message.
> > > Best,
> > > Dilsad

messages.subject: Access previous values of nodes
messages.subject_clean: Access previous values of nodes
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

what is the best way to handle access to previous values of nodes? I mean not only the current value of the chain, but all values. Something like

values(models, nodes, iterations)

Is this possible with a user-written sampler by accessing the modelValues object appropriately? Or is it even possible with a user-written distribution (that depends on past values) that could then be used with all standard samplers?

-----------------------------

Probably irrelevant background:

I am working on a Quasi-Bayesian/Laplace-type approach to Generalized Method of Moments estimation. The basic idea is to substitute the likelihood in an MCMC procedure with a quasi-likelihood that is motivated by the CLT on the moments of a given model.

Consider a moment function m(θ) with parameter θ . One would specify a “quasi-likelihood” with average moments m and weighting matrix W as
p(D|θ)∼exp(m^T W m).

and estimate the “quasi-posterior” with a MCMC procedure.

The problem I have is that the weighting matrix W should be the inverse of a consistent covariance estimate of the moments at the true parameter. As this parameter is unknown, one usually relies on iterative procedures. One solution is to take a covariance estimator using the posterior mean of the preceding chain.

messages.subject: Re: Access previous values of nodes
messages.subject_clean: Access previous values of nodes
messages.body_plain:
Hi Patrick,

This sounds very interesting.  I'm going to give some fairly high-level answers and am happy to dig into details later if it helps.

The short answer is no, but there are several ways you could use tricks to access what you want.  I'll also point you to some source code.

The main nimbleFunction driving the MCMC iterations is returned from buildMCMC.  It's in MCMC_build.R and is, I hope, somewhat readable.  There are two (or three) modelValues objects created in its setup code.  mvSaved has only one set of all model variables.  That is used to hold the "current" state of the model for purposes of steps such as Metropolis-Hastings accept/reject.  mvSamples is where the MCMC output is stored.  (mvSamples2 is the potential third one involved, which also stores MCMC output if a monitors2 and optionally thin2 are defined, but this doesn't seem important to discuss.).  Importantly, only buildMCMC (but not the samplers) uses mvSamples.  Normally, each sampler only uses mvSaved but does not have access to mvSamples.  So that is why in normal operation, samplers can't look at past states of the chain.

Here are several ways you could use some flexibility to do it.  First, you could have a sampler create its own modelValues or more simply its own matrix and store a history of states on its own.  This would be independent of whatever is being stored in mvSamples.  This (using a matrix) is the approach used for adaptation (self-tuning) in a block (multivariate) MH sampler, so you could look at sampler_RW_block in MCMC_samplers.R to see how it's done there.  See the empirSamp matrix.

Second, you could have a sampler (that you write) call back to R using a nimbleRcall.  From R, you are free to access the compiled MCMC object, including its mvStates.  This would not be the most efficient approach, since going into R evaluation is always slower and you'd be extracting the mvStates matrix anew every time.  But it would work and if you are more worried about methodology than computational efficiency right now, it might be your easiest option.

Third, you could write a sampler and have its setup code look up into its calling environment (parent.frame()) and find mvSamples there.  Then if you use mvSamples in run code, the nimble compiler should arrange for your sampler to be accessing the compiled modelValues object from the MCMC driving function (the buildMCMC object).  This would be tricky, non-standard, and I could imagine circumstances where it could be confusing to an end user.  However again if your goal is a research system, it might work.

I hope one or more of these ideas helps!

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Indeed it seems to be a statistical estimate issue more than a nimble issue per se.  You could try using block samplers for highly correlated dimensions, but you would want to be sure the two years of CAR models are not, as you note as a potential issue, causing some estimation (or other) problem.

On Tue, Dec 7, 2021 at 1:47 AM 'David Pleydell' via nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com> wrote:

> Dear Dan
>
> I have only looked at your trace plots and have not looked at the details of your model. But it is quite clear that there are very strong correlations between certain pairs of parameters. Have you tried the cross-correlation plot in the coda package? I suspect if you do then you'll see correlations very close to one - because some parameters have near identical trace plots.  These very strong relations  suggest non-identifiability in your model. This would point to a need to re-parameterise things a little bit.
>
> Hope that helps
> David
>
>
> On Tuesday, 7 December 2021 at 02:30:28 UTC+1 drfi...@gmail.com wrote:
> > Perry,
> > Thanks for getting back to me. You are correct, the chains were short just as an example of the  model. As you noted the mark-recapture part of the model is converging. Per your suggestions, I modified the code to run the chains in parallel, initialized more parameters, ran the model for more iterations (niter=210000, nburnin=10000, thin=100) with convergence issues (Rhat > 1.2 and n.eff<100) for some parameters in the proper CAR model.  There is poor mixing of the chains in gamma[2], sig[1], sig[2], and cor12. I pasted the CAR part of the code below.  As a reminder the parameter phi =  log of fish density. See attached trace and density plots..
> >
> > One issue may be that I have not correctly implemented the CAR model for both years, as it was adapted from another source and may also need more informative priors. Thought? Thanks again for your help.
> > Dan
> >
> > ##############################################################
> >   #Proper CAR Model
> >   for (h in 1:yrs){
> >     S[h,1:s] ~ dcar_proper(mumod[1:s],C[1:L],adj[1:L],num[1:s],M[1:s],tauS[h],gamma[h]) #car proper use with build
> >     tauS[h]<-1
> >     gamma[h]~dunif(bou[1],bou[2])
> >   }
> >
> >   #Wishart priors & equation for phi
> >   Prec[1:yrs,1:yrs]~dwish(R[1:yrs,1:yrs],yrs)
> >   Cov[1:yrs,1:yrs]<-inverse(Prec[1:yrs,1:yrs])
> >   Achol[1:yrs,1:yrs]<-t(chol(Cov[1:yrs,1:yrs]))
> >   for(i in 1:s){
> >     phi[1:yrs,i]<-Achol[1:yrs,1:yrs]%*%S[1:yrs,i]
> >     }
> >
> > #Derived parameters
> >   sig[1]<-sqrt(Cov[1,1])
> >   sig[2]<-sqrt(Cov[2,2])
> >   cor12<-Cov[1,2]/(sig[1]*sig[2])
> > ###############################################
> >
> >
> > On Mon, Nov 15, 2021 at 3:36 PM Perry de Valpine <pdeva...@berkeley.edu> wrote:
> > > Hi Dan,
> > >
> > > I looked through your code and ran it.  I don't know this model well, but I think I roughly followed it.
> > >
> > > I don't see something that is not working in terms of MCMC machinery or obvious changes in strategy.  Your chains looked very short to me.  I ran them for much longer (10x, and you might consider 100x), with some thinning (and possibly use monitors2 as well), and lots of nodes seemed to be mixing.
> > >
> > > I did not see mixing for most of the theta elements, but that seemed to make sense.  It looks like those are sets of Dirichlet-distributed vectors with priors making it extremely likely that there is no movement between strata, so there will be one 1 and the rest 0, or nearly so, in each vector.  That makes sense because the data seem to show only a handful of movements between strata.  I am not clear if there is much information in the data on movement and hence much useful estimation that can happen here or if you are comfortable more or less imposing the movement probabilities or if I'm not following this part.  But from an MCMC perspective, it seems to make sense that when there are mostly 0s for how many fish moved strata, and when the prior says strongly that there is nearly no chance of moving, then the posterior will say there is nearly no chance of moving, and all of those theta elements be essentially 0 all the time.  If I look at a cell of theta corresponding (I think) to some of the few movements in the data (e.g. "theta[2, 4, 7]"), it mixes with non-zero probabilities.
> > >
> > > It can be important to initialize all unobserved nodes, but sometimes it works fine not to.
> > >
> > > HTH
> > >

> > > >
> > > > Model
> > > > A study was conducted on a stream with 17 contiguous strata, where juvenile salmonids were captured, marked, and released. The stream was resampled at a later time where fish marked and unmarked fish were enumerated. If there was no movement between strata, this could be analyzed using a simple Lincoln/Petersen closed population model. However, there was movement between strata and a better approach is to analyzed the data using a Darroch model, which is a multistate model that allows movement or transition between the strata.
> > > >
> > > > Rather than estimate strata adundance (n*) directly, we assume the abundance is a Poisson distributed based on the product of the density (fish/meter) and the area in meters of each strata. I could analyze this as a hierarchical model where log(lambda[i])~Normal(mu_phi,tau_phi). However, this would not account for spatial dependence between adjacent stream reaches, which can be analyzed using a proper CAR model.
> > > >

The current model has very high autocorrelation, low effective sample size. and poor convergence. Given the model complexity, I could not initialize all nodes and settled for one that would not crash the model. I would appreciate any advice on different samplers or code modification that would improve convergence and speed but am at a loss on where to start given the different distributions and my inexperience with NIMBLE. Dear nimble developers, dear users,

I encountered another error which I am completely clueless about:

Defining model
Error in BUGSdecl$targetIndexNamePieces[[iDim]] : subscript out of bounds

It's gonna be something with the indices, but my code is more than hundred lines long, and contains a lot of indexed arrays. How am I supposed to find where the problem is from this message? This frustration reminds me old times with WinBUGS and the infamous Trap 66 :-)) I really appreciate the helpfulness of the authors here in the forum, but I cannot be sending code here every time I get an error. I am trying to find for myself a sustainable way to develop models in Nimble. How are other users coping with this? Nimble is out for 7+ years, right? How come no one became frustrated enough yet to invest time in this? Wouldn't it save development time in the end?

Would it be difficult to implement, to report line numbers and node names?

I am C++ & R developer myself, so I think it might save me time and nerves to contribute this to Nimble myself. Note that for some errors, not only line numbers but also node names would be very helpful (see e.g. the infamous "Invalid parent values" in JAGS, frustrated me enough that I once patched my JAGS to report more details on this).

Thank you and wish you beautiful advent time.

Tomas

Hi Perry,

Thanks again for your help. I've re-defined my density function to return a scalar, as you advised, since I will be using it in a model.
Following your advice, my random sampling function for the distribution now compiles and appears to work as expected. Thanks for pointing out the existance of rcat as a more elegant alternative to rmulti for this application.

My function now looks like this:

rdiscnorm <- nimbleFunction (
  run = function (n = double(0, default = 1),
                  mean = double(0, default = 0),
                  sd = double(0, default = 1),
                  min = double(0),
                  max = double(0)) {

    if (n < 0) nimStop("invalid argument x < 0")

    returnType(double(0))
    prob <- numeric(length = length(min:max))
    for (i in seq_along((min:max))) {
      prob[i] <- ddiscnorm((min:max)[i], mean, sd, min, max)
    }
    return((min:max)[rcat(prob = prob)])

})
rdiscnormC <- compileNimble(rdiscnorm, showCompilerOutput = TRUE)

Now on to the p and q functions. I'll post another question if I run into more trouble.

Cheers,
Gregory

messages.body_plain:
Hi Tomas,

In cases where NIMBLE traps an error, we generally try to report information about the problematic code, though I can't say we're perfect about it. In this case, the error is being reported by R, which means we haven't trapped it ourselves; i.e., something is going wrong that we haven't anticipated. }

 }

defining model...

checking model sizes and dimensions... This model is not fully initialized. This is not an error. To see which variables are not initialized, use model$initializeInfo(). For more information on model initialization, see help(modelInitialization).

Marcin

messages.body_plain:
Marcin, I think the issue comes down to a lack of initialization of the multivariate normal precision matrices, specifically:

taur[1:2,1:2]
tauv[1:2,1:2]
tauge[1:2,1:2]

Try adding initial values for these, which would be any positive definite 2x2 matrices.  The identity matrix would be fine.  This will give them valid initial states, but they will still undergo MCMC sampling.  Notice that in NIMBLE, fixed "data" is different from "initial values".  You can add these initial values as shown below (new code is in blue):

modelConsts<-list(N=N,ne=ne,nv=nv,nr=nr,rep=c(rep),env=c(env),sys=c(sys),v=c(v))
modelData<-list(y=c(y))
modelInits <- list(taur = diag(2), tauv = diag(2), taure = diag(2))
mod <- nimbleModel(code = model, name = "model", constants = modelConsts, data = modelData, inits = modelInits)

You could also consider providing neutral initial values for the other model parameters, as well, such as "a", "tau", and others.

Give this a go, and see if it works now.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody!

I am trying to introduce an optimization function inside my Nimble model, but I am having some problems with that. I tried to follow the information provided at Nimble guide.

This is my function to optimize. It is intended to provide a gamma fit to raw data. Par has a length of two and provides the shape and rate parameters for the gamma distribution. Also, dcc can be easily simulated if you wish:

dcc <- rgamma(1e3, 1.5, 0.01)

objectiveFunction <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(par = double(1), dcc = double(1)){

    t1a <- sum(log(dcc))
    t2a <- sum(dcc)
    obs2 <- length(dcc)
    a  <- par[1]
    b <- par[2]

    returnType(double(0))
    return( - ((a - 1) * t1a - b * t2a - obs2 * a * log(1/b) - obs2 * log(gamma(a))))
   }
)

objectiveFunction(c(1,0.1), dcc) #The function works

Here's the optimizer:

optimizer <- nimbleFunction(

  run = function(method = character(0), fnscale = double(0), dcc = double(1), lower = double(1)){

    control <- optimDefaultControl()
    control$fnscale <- fnscale
    par <- c(1,0.01)
    return(optim(par, objectiveFunction, method = method, lower = lower, control = control, dcc  = dcc))
    returnType(optimResultNimbleList())
  }
)

optimizer(method = "L-BFGS-B", dcc = dcc, lower = c(0.0001, 0.0001), fnscale = 1) #The function works properly and the results are realistic.

Everything seems to work fine until when I try to compile the function to use it in my models.

cOptimizer <- compileNimble(optimizer)

I get an error output:
" Failed to create the shared library. Run 'printErrors()' to see the compilation errors."

By checking the output briefly, one thing the compiler is complaining about is:

"error: no matching function for call to 'nimOptim(NimArr<1, double>&, double (&)(NimArr<1, double>&, NimArr<1, double>&), const char [5], NimArr<1, double>&, std::__cxx11::string&, NimArr<1, double>&, double&, nimSmartPtr<OptimControlNimbleList>&, bool)'
 return(nimOptim(par, rcFun_R_GlobalEnv37, "NULL", ARG3_dcc_, ARG1_method_, ARG4_lower_, Inf, control, false));"

I feel a little bit lost as the function appears to work but fails to be compiled. Does anyone have any hints on why this is happening?

Thanks for your time and have a happy new year!

Jaume

messages.subject: Re: Question on Error in chol.default(model$taur[1:2, 1:2])
messages.subject_clean: Question on Error in chol.default(model$taur[1:2, 1:2])
messages.body_plain:
Yes, briefly, under the hood NIMBLE transforms model distributions to a "canonical" parmeterization.  For the dmnorm distribution, this canonical parameterization is always in terms of the Cholesky decomposition of either the covariance matrix, or the precision matrix (depending on which was provided in the original dmnorm declaration.

That is, if you specify precision, then NIMBLE changes this line:
... ~ dmnorm(mu[1:k], Q[1:k,1:k])
into this:
... ~ dmnorm(mu[1:k], cholesky = chol(Q[1:k,1:k]), prec_param = 1)   ## prec_param = 1 indicates that the "cholesky" argument is the factorization of the precision

Or, if you specify dmnorm in terms of covariance, then NIMBLE changes this line:
... ~ dmnorm(mu[1:k], cov = Sigma[1:k,1:k])
into this:
... ~ dmnorm(mu[1:k], cholesky = chol(Sigma[1:k,1:k]), prec_param = 0)   ## prec_param = 0 indicates that the "cholesky" argument is the factorization of the covariance

So, yes, if you want  you can specify the dmnorm model declaration directly using either canonical parameterization, just provide the mean vector, the (upper) triangular cholesky factor matrix as the "cholesky" parameter, and then provide prec_param = 0 or 1, depending on whether the "cholesky" argument is the factorization of the precision (1) or the covariance (0) matrix.

As for multiple initial values: the list you supply to nimbleModel must only be a single list of initial values - for example, your "inits1" object.  Nimble will create the (single) model using these initial values.  For supplying different initial values for multiple chains, you would subsequently pass your "modelInits" (a list of lists of initial values) as the "inits" argument to either nimbleMCMC() or runMCMC() function, also specifying the nchains argument.  A good workflow for you might be to use nimbleModel to create the model, then buildMCMC to build an MCMC, then using compileNimble() to compile both the model and the MCMC, and finally runMCMC (along with the list of different initial values) to run the compiled MCMC.

Hope this helps, keep at it,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hello Nimble users,

I've created a custom distribution including a nimbleFunction for each d, r, p, and q functions. Those functions all compile successfully using compileNimble, and I'm able to register the distribution using registerDistributions. However, when used in a model the MCMC is much slower than when using one of Nimble's provided distributions. I'd like to speed it up, if possible, so I'm trying to identify why it's so slow. I see two likely culprits.

1) The model is using the un-compiled distribution functions. This seems possible, because the calls in the model code use the un-compiled versions. I did this because when I try to register the compiled distribution or use it in a model, I get the an error that the function is not available and "must be a nimbleFunction (with no setup code)." But since I'm using a compiled model and mcmc, I'm guessing that the Nimble functions for my distribution get compiled at the same time, but I'm not sure about that. So, could someone tell me whether that is the case, and if it is not, then how do I use compiled versions of my functions in the model?

2) If the model is using compiled versions of my distribution functions, then the slowness is caused by how I've implemented the function. If that's the case, I'll need to think about how that might be improved. I have a good guess where the problem would be, but whether that can be eliminated might be a topic for a separate post here.

Thanks in advance,
Gregory

messages.body_plain:
Short answer to (1) is that yes, when you compile the model, it also compiles any user-defined distributions or functions which are in the model, and the compiled model object will be using the compiled versions of your custom distributions.

I hope you can make some headway with (2).  Yes, depending on how you've written things can cause non-trivial performance gains / losses.  You might also think about any memory allocation which has to take place (of vectors / arrays / higher dimensional objects) which might be invoked on *every * call to your distribution, which is one possible pitfall.  For example if you create a new array variable inside your distribution, then this memory allocation will happen, repeatedly, on every call of your distribution.

Keep at it,
Daniel

Daniel,

Thanks for the insight; I think it suggests something to try. My distribution is a discretized version of a normal distribution. The implementation of the d function is essentially this:

1) Define a finite range of support for the distribution.
2) Create a vector of normal densities for all integers within the range.
3) Standardize the vector created in (2) by dividing each element by the sum of its elements.
4) Look up the vector element corresponding to a particular integer and return it.

(2) Has to be done each time the density function is called, and if the distribution has a large range of support, then that's a lot of calls to repeat. An obvious solution in C++ is to create something like a std::map where key={integer in range}, value={corresponding element from standardized vector in (3)} and store that map for future use. I'm not sure how to do that with Nimble, though.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jaume,

nimOptim does not support the ... argument and so there is no ability for you to pass "dcc" as an argument in the way you are doing it. We have some brief information in Section 11.2.8 of the nimble manual about how to handle that. So please take a look and let us know if you have questions.

Another option may be to use nimbleRcall and just call R's optim directly from within an R function that is called via nimbleRcall from a nimbleFunction that is used in your nimble model.

-chris
